title: Hotel Key Card Artwork And Printing Checklist
summary: A production-ready artwork and print checklist for hotel key cards that walks branding, numbering, finish, substrate tolerances, proof review and front-desk handling into one document — so artwork moves on a passed compatibility brief rather than blocking it.
heroPoints: Artwork moves fastest when compatibility and numbering rules are already stable — otherwise every revision triggers a repeat tool-up.
A hotel key card has to serve branding, front-desk issue flow and replacement handling at the same time; any artwork that wins on only one of them fails in operation.
A clean checklist prevents revision loops and produces a proof the brand team and the operations team can both approve on the first review.

sections.title: What a production-ready hotel card brief looks like
sections.intro: The first print brief is the document that decides whether the proof cycle takes ten days or six weeks. A complete brief answers every question a production planner would otherwise ask.
bullets: Card format: CR80 landscape (most hotels) or CR80 portrait (occasional boutique). Rounded corner radius (3.18 mm is standard). Substrate and thickness carried forward from the material selection decision.
Print faces: front-only, front-and-back, or full-bleed wrap. Specify which face carries the room number, loyalty tier, or regulatory text.
Colour spec: CMYK with Pantone references for any spot colours that must hit exactly (hotel group reds, luxury blacks, foil golds).
Fonts: embedded and outlined on every AI or PDF delivery. Do not rely on the supplier having the foundry license.
Print method: offset, digital, UV, dye-sub, screen print, thermal transfer — dictated by the substrate and by the finish stack.
Finish stack: matte or gloss lamination, spot UV, foil stamping, embossing, laser engraving. Declare the order of operations, since finishes interact.
Bleed and safe area: 2 mm bleed, 3 mm safe area. Non-negotiable. Artwork that ignores the safe area runs into the corner-rounding path.

sections.title: Numbering rules that actually survive production
sections.intro: Serial numbering is where artwork meets operations. Get it wrong and the front desk ends up hand-writing room numbers on the card sleeve.
bullets: Unique serials: decide whether every card carries a unique printed number, and whether that number is visible to the guest or hidden (UV ink, rear-face small type, thermal print overlay).
Room-range numbering: some properties print the room number on the card. This ties inventory tightly to room mapping — any room renumbering project has to re-order cards.
Loyalty-tier variants: gold, platinum, suite and club-floor cards often carry different artwork. Decide up-front how many variants the supplier produces, and how re-ordering per variant works.
Variable-data printing capability: UV digital printers handle variable data well; offset printers do not. If numbering is variable, the print method is effectively chosen for you.

Checksum alignment: if the PMS expects a specific serial format (printed number must equal encoded serial, or a derived checksum), document that in the brief. Numbering mismatches are the single most common reason for re-issue confusion at the desk.

sections.title: Substrate-specific artwork tolerances
sections.intro: PVC is forgiving. Wood, PLA and bio-composite are not. Artwork has to be designed for the substrate, not adapted to it later.
bullets: PVC: full CMYK with heavy coverage, fine detail at 300 dpi, small type down to 5 pt readable. Recycled PVC tolerates the same specifications with a slight fidelity reduction on dark coverage.

Wood: laser engraving gives crisp monochrome results but loses photographic detail. UV printing with a white base layer restores colour but hides the grain. Decide which signal matters — grain or photography — before the artwork round starts.
PLA: keep print temperatures below 60 °C, avoid large solid dark areas that trap heat, allow for slightly softer colour registration than PVC.
Bio-composite: coarse visible fibres mean small type below 7 pt becomes unreliable. Lean on typography-driven designs, not photographic ones.
Stone paper: matte finish by default, does not take gloss lamination well, tolerates photographic artwork but in a muted palette.

sections.title: Finish interactions that bite in the proof round
sections.intro: The difference between a beautiful proof and a problematic proof is usually the interaction of two or more finishes. These are the ones worth knowing about before the proof arrives.
bullets: Spot UV over foil stamp: the UV usually bonds less well to the foil than to the laminate. Specify foil first, laminate over, then spot UV on the laminated surface — not directly on the foil.
Embossing over full-bleed dark print: embossing can crack heavy ink coverage. Design a slight clear zone around the emboss area, or accept a visible cracking pattern.
Soft-touch laminate over digital print: the laminate can amplify colour shifts from the digital press. Always press-check a laminated proof, not a bare digital print.
Laser engraving on pre-printed wood: the engraving removes the print layer. Specify engraving zones as artwork voids so the engraver does not clip the logo.
Magnetic-stripe compatibility: some legacy lock estates still carry a magnetic stripe alongside the chip. A stripe constrains the back-face artwork and rules out embossing in that zone.

sections.title: Proof review: what to actually check when the sample arrives
sections.intro: A proof review that only checks colour and copy misses the operational and compliance issues that block production. Use this checklist instead.
bullets: Colour: check against the approved Pantone references under D50 lighting, not office fluorescents. Colour that reads right under a warm-lobby lamp can read cold under daylight.
Copy: proofread legal text, loyalty-programme terms, and room-numbering format. Verify non-English characters if international.
Numbering: confirm the printed serial matches the encoded serial in the way the PMS expects.
Compatibility: try the proof card on the real lock, not just a reference reader. Wood and PLA cards can pass reference and fail lock.
Handling: ride the card in a staff pocket for 48 hours. If the finish scuffs, the guest will see the same scuff in week one.
Encoder handling: confirm the card feeds reliably through the front-desk encoder. Thick wood cards sometimes jam on older encoders.
Regulatory: confirm any required compliance marks (FSC logo on certified wood, GRS on recycled PVC, compostability logo on PLA) are present and legible.

sections.title: Artwork sign-off workflow across three stakeholders
sections.intro: Hotel card artwork almost always involves three approvers: brand (marketing/creative), operations (front desk/housekeeping), and compliance (legal/sustainability). A linear sign-off workflow prevents conflicting feedback.
bullets: Step 1 — brand lock: marketing approves concept, colour, finish direction. No operational review yet. Timebox this to five business days.

Step 2 — operations review: front desk and housekeeping confirm numbering, loyalty variants, and replacement-card simplicity. Change requests here almost always override brand preferences that cause issue-flow friction.
Step 3 — compliance sign-off: sustainability claims, trademark use, and any jurisdiction-specific text (language, privacy notice). Compliance reviews the final composite, not the brand-only proof.
Step 4 — supplier proof: the physical proof goes through all three approvers again as a single composite review. Any divergence resets the cycle.
Documentation: each sign-off is captured with approver name, date and the exact asset version. Weeks later when someone asks 'why does the card say X', the log answers in one line.

sections.title: Packaging, delivery and the first 48 hours at the property
sections.intro: Artwork quality fails most often in the last inch: the sleeve, the courier box and the front-desk drawer. These are the details that separate a clean handover from a scramble.
bullets: Sleeves: decide whether cards ship in branded sleeves, plain sleeves, or loose. Branded sleeves add cost and delivery time; loose cards save both but risk handling damage in transit.

Bundling: most properties want cards bundled in 100s or 250s, with a coversheet showing serial range and loyalty variant. Large chains standardise bundle size group-wide; boutique properties improvise.
Shipping protection: wood, PLA and bio-composite cards need more protective packaging than PVC. Specify double-wall cartons and desiccant for humid destinations.
First-48 storage: confirm with operations where the cards go on arrival. A sunlit lobby cabinet is enough to fade PLA in two weeks.

First-issue audit: the first 50 cards issued from the new stock should be audited for print defects, serial mismatches and finish problems. If defects appear, stop issue and call the supplier before the front desk burns through the order.

Re-order trigger: set a replenishment threshold at the property that triggers the next order before stock runs below a defensible reserve. Premium materials with longer lead times need higher thresholds.

faq.question: When should hotel teams start detailed artwork work?
faq.answer: After the card format, chip family, compatibility path and numbering rules are locked. Starting artwork before these are stable almost always forces a repeat revision cycle because one upstream change (chip family, card thickness, serial format) invalidates design decisions downstream.

faq.question: What does a useful hotel card print checklist actually include?
faq.answer: Card format and thickness, print faces, colour spec with Pantone references, font licensing, print method, finish stack, bleed and safe area, numbering rules, loyalty variants, substrate-specific tolerances, compliance marks, packaging format, and a named approver for each sign-off step. A brief missing any of these items is the reason the proof cycle takes six weeks instead of ten days.

faq.question: Does a printed serial number have to match the encoded serial?
faq.answer: Only if the PMS workflow expects them to match. Some properties use the printed number only for the front desk to distinguish cards in a stack, while encoding uses a different serial. Others require the two to match so the PMS re-issue flow works from the printed number. Decide this during the encoding brief, not during artwork.

faq.question: What finish combinations cause the most proof problems?
faq.answer: Spot UV over foil stamping is the most common issue because the UV layer bonds less well to the foil than to the laminate. The fix is to stamp the foil first, laminate over it, and apply spot UV on the laminated surface. Embossing over heavy dark ink is the second most common; leave a clear zone around the emboss or accept visible ink cracking.

faq.question: How does artwork change for wood or PLA cards?
faq.answer: Wood loses photographic detail under laser engraving and hides grain under UV-printed white bases; decide which signal matters before artwork starts. PLA tolerates fewer finishing temperatures and dislikes heavy dark coverage. Bio-composite loses readability on small type. The material decision should be locked before artwork, because artwork that works on PVC often does not work on wood.

faq.question: Who has to sign off on hotel card artwork?
faq.answer: Three stakeholder groups: brand (marketing/creative), operations (front desk/housekeeping), and compliance (legal/sustainability). A linear workflow — brand lock, operations review, compliance sign-off, physical proof review — prevents the cross-team conflict that causes the most proof delays. Capture each sign-off with name, date and asset version.

faq.question: What is the most common avoidable mistake in hotel card artwork?
faq.answer: Pushing full artwork revisions before the card format, chip family and numbering rules are stable. Every upstream change forces an artwork change, which forces a proof change, which forces another sample cycle. Stabilise compatibility and numbering first, then artwork moves on a predictable cadence.
